candidates.name: Factitious disorder
support_spans: Clues suggesting volitional behavior included selective acceptance of benzodiazepines and gabapentin while refusing other medications, eating all meals despite “stupor,” abruptly lapsing into and out of catatonia-like and psychotic behaviors depending on the topic of conversation, purposeful movements to obtain lorazepam after seizures, and evidence of self‐induced urinary incontinence during one episode.
candidates.why: The patient's behavior and response to medication suggest a pattern of factitious behavior.

candidates.why: The patient's behavior and response to medication suggest a pattern of malingering.

candidates.name: Conversion disorder
support_spans: Catatonia-like signs: flat affect with psychomotor retardation and fluctuating mutism; complete lack of social contact; twitching, eye grimacing, and shoulder shrugging; posturing and immobility; diaphoresis.
Seizure-like behavior: episodes of head jerking with eye fluttering without tongue biting; remained conversant; benign neurologic examination.
contradict_spans: A regional catatonia specialist evaluated her and noted that she was unlikely to have catatonia.
candidates.why: The patient's symptoms suggest a conversion disorder, but the catatonia specialist's evaluation and the patient's response to medication raise doubts.

key_evidence_spans: Clues suggesting volitional behavior included selective acceptance of benzodiazepines and gabapentin while refusing other medications, eating all meals despite “stupor,” abruptly lapsing into and out of catatonia-like and psychotic behaviors depending on the topic of conversation, purposeful movements to obtain lorazepam after seizures, and evidence of self‐induced urinary incontinence during one episode.
A regional catatonia specialist evaluated her and noted that she was unlikely to have catatonia.
Repeated lorazepam challenge tests had limited effect on her behaviors and appeared to reinforce them.
